problem: LLM-based VLN agents such as MapGPT work in simulators but suffer severe spatial hallucination in real-world deployment (repeated paths, collisions, premature stopping) because they rely on a single cue system or a single map and a single-expert decision process.
motivation: Real-world navigation needs precise directional control, and similar viewpoints are hard to tell apart, so single-expert LLM agents lose spatial awareness. The paper takes inspiration from biological spatial cognition (hippocampal place/grid cells, head-direction cells, parietal integration) to give LLM agents multi-level, dynamically updated spatial memory.
key_idea: BrainNav is a bio-inspired zero-shot LLM/VLM navigation framework with five brain-like modules that combines a dual map (coordinate + topological) with dual orientation (relative + absolute) and memory-based backtracking to reduce spatial hallucination.
insight: The ablation removes each module in turn: without the parietal spatial builder (maps) SR falls to 0%, without the memory center SR falls to 23.7%, and without the prefrontal decision center it falls to 44.6%. This suggests that explicit spatial structure and memory, rather than a bigger LLM, are what keep a GPT-4o agent from hallucinating in the real world. The backtracking rate (10% vs 75% for MapGPT) supports the same reading. Note that ablations of the perception and execution modules dropping to 0% mostly reflect that the pipeline cannot run without them.
method: Hippocampal Memory Center (HMC): stores the topological map (as a dictionary) and the history of actions and images, and reuses stored trajectories. It finds the fewest-step backtracking path by graph search and can bypass high-level reasoning when a matching past trajectory exists.

Visual Cortex Perception Engine (VCPE): a VLM processes images from four directions in stages (object/semantic list, traversable-area labeling, relative distance estimation) to give structured perception input.

Parietal Spatial Builder (PSB): builds a coordinate map by adding four candidate points around the current position according to orientation (θ+i·90°), each with a unique ID. It also builds a topological graph G=(V,E) with adjacency/roadgraph updates, and supplies connectivity, unvisited nodes and action options to the planner.
Prefrontal Decision Center (PDC): an LLM (GPT-4o) fuses memory, perception and map information into task decisions, a subsequent action plan and a list of motor commands.

Cerebellar Motion Execution Unit (CMEU): converts high-level commands into predefined macro actions (forward, turn left/right, backward, stop, backtrack). It uses relative orientation for general motion and absolute orientation (0° = North, coordinate differences Δx, Δy) for backtracking.

numbers_note: No standard simulator benchmark (R2R etc.) is evaluated; all results come from the authors' own real-world lab test with a custom instruction set. Backtracking rate is 10% and BSCR is 73.3% (Table 3). The ablation SRs (0%, 0%, 44.6%, 23.7%, 0%) are given only in text, without a table.
results: On the authors' real-world lab test, BrainNav reaches 88% SR / 82 SPL on targeted search and 71% SR on path navigation, against 0% and 14% for MapGPT. It outperforms MapGPT on all four complex task types (e.g. 87.5% SR on obstacle avoidance vs 0%), and its backtracking rate is 10% vs 75%.
limitations: Evaluated only on a single lab environment with a self-designed instruction set and one weak baseline (MapGPT). No standard benchmarks or other real-robot baselines are compared, and no statistical detail is reported.
Low success on multi-target (35%) and interaction/person-following (25%) tasks, and instability with dynamic obstacles.
Depends on a proprietary GPT-4o; coordinate maps use coarse 90° discrete moves and a step size stated as 0.5 cm (likely a typo), and the ablation reports SR without a table.
